name: PT Roda Vivatex Tbk

frontmatter.title: Roda Vivatex: a net-cash office landlord at a discount, with a split as the catalyst
frontmatter.summary: Roda Vivatex owns four Jakarta office towers outright, carries no debt and holds cash equal to a large slice of its market value, yet trades at 0.9x book and 9.4x earnings. Restating the depreciation the data pack misses turns the economics into a 76.0% EBITDA-margin annuity. We rate it HOLD with a Rp12,039 target.
thesis: The asset value is real and the market is not paying for it: our RNAV method carries Rp16,249 a share against Rp12,350, and even after the engine's 30.0% illiquidity haircut the twelve-month target is Rp12,039, a 2.3% total return including the Rp594 dividend [S19, S0].

The data pack understates the cost base: it shows a depreciation line of under a billion rupiah, while the LK charges IDR85.5bn of investment-property depreciation inside operational costs, so true EBITDA is IDR433.1bn not IDR347.6bn [S19, F9].
The final tax on leasing is levied on gross rental revenue, above the operating line, so profit grows more slowly than revenue and the tax cannot be deferred against losses [S19 p.14, p.47].
The one-for-twenty split approved on 4 November 2026 is the nearest dated catalyst: it targets a stock that turns over IDR47.0m a day, and the controller keeps 42.5% of the enlarged count [S2, F27].

The bear case is a tenant-retention and cap-rate story, not a balance-sheet one: the largest tenant is 19.5% of revenue and the portfolio has no disclosed occupancy, so we cannot verify the buildings are holding their share of a market that is still 25.7% vacant [S19, S15].

catalysts.event: EGM approved the one-for-twenty stock split; watch the new-share listing date and the resulting liquidity
Colliers' third-quarter Jakarta office report: CBD occupancy holding near three-quarters and a vacancy path falling through 2029
FY2026 audited LK and the FY2026 dividend resolution, the first test of the split-era payout

blocks.text: We initiate on Roda Vivatex at **HOLD** with a twelve-month target of Rp12,039 against a last price of Rp12,350: a 2.3% total return including the Rp594 dividend we expect over the year, a forward yield of 4.8%. Every per-share figure in this report is on the pre-split count of 268.8m shares, because the traded price and the data pack still are; after the one-for-twenty split approved on 4 November 2026 the same values divide by twenty [S2, S0].

The variant view is not that the stock is cheap. It is that the market is charging the right kind of discount for the wrong size of one. RDTX owns four Jakarta office buildings with no debt, no development risk and cash that is a material fraction of its market capitalisation [S19 p.13, S7]. On our cap rate the recurring gross profit alone capitalises to more than the enterprise value, which is why the RNAV leg of our valuation lands at Rp16,249 a share even after we take 15.0% off for the control structure [S19, S0]. The stock trades at 0.9x book — book being original cost, not appraisal — and 9.4x forward earnings for a business whose EBITDA margin we put at 76.0% [S19].

Two things move the value from here. The first is the discount itself: we assume it narrows by only a few points over the year, and the engine then applies its own 30.0% illiquidity haircut on top, because IDR47.0m of daily turnover cannot absorb institutional size [S0]. The second is the office cycle, which is turning unevenly: CBD occupancy is 76.3%, Grade A 78.0% and Premium 84.0%, with vacancy forecast to fall from 25.7% to 21.1% by 2029 [S15]. RDTX owns the vintage that wins when tenants pay for quality and loses when they pay only for price.

What we would not claim is precision on the buildings. The company does not publish portfolio occupancy or rent rolls, so our revenue base is the audited P&L and our cap rate is a market judgement, not an appraisal [S19, S15]. The largest tenant, Pertamina Hulu Energi, is 19.5% of revenue [S19 p.79]. That concentration, and the final tax levied on gross rent rather than profit, are the two facts a reader should keep in view when they look at the target.

The rating is HOLD rather than BUY because the discount we are underwriting is a twelve-month, catalyst-dependent narrowing, not convergence: with 42.5% in the hands of the controller and a float of 21.1%, nothing forces the gap to close on our schedule [S2]. We would add on evidence that the split has actually deepened liquidity, or on a portfolio occupancy disclosure.

Roda Vivatex is a Jakarta office landlord with a textile history. It was founded as a polyester fabric producer, listed in 1990, and only moved into property through a subsidiary from 2002; the textile factory was closed in 2014 and the group has been a rent collector since [S6, S19 p.19]. It owns four office buildings: Menara Mandiri Inhealth and Menara RDTX Square on Jalan Prof. Dr. Satrio, Menara PHE on Jalan TB Simatupang, and RDTX Place on the Satrio corridor, the newest of the four [S7, S10]. The head office sits on an upper floor of RDTX Square, which tells you what the business is: a single-asset-class owner-operator, not a developer [S7].

The revenue mix is that of a serviced landlord, not a developer. Rent was IDR293.7bn of the IDR570.2bn booked in FY2025; maintenance and power — the service charge that tenants pay for the building they occupy — was IDR242.8bn; parking and overtime made up most of the rest [S19 p.79]. There are no marketing sales, no handovers and no land bank: every parcel the group owns in Jakarta is built and let, which is why our RNAV carries no separate land value [S19 p.62]. The residual income lines that our template labels as development revenue are the LK's own "others" bucket of under a billion rupiah a year, and we say so rather than dressing them up as sales.

Group structure is simple and wholly controlled. PT Chitatex Peni, the rump textile entity, is wholly owned in all but a nominal fraction and reduces to little more than a shell; PT Chitaland Perkasa owns and operates RDTX Place, with total assets of IDR1,706.1bn at the end of FY2025, and is owned outright [S19 p.20, p.22]. Both are consolidated, minority interests are nil, and essentially all profit accrues to the parent's shareholders [S19 p.13]. That matters for the valuation: there is no holdco leak, no minority to deduct, and no joint venture whose cash we cannot see.

Tenancy is corporate and scattered. The customer note shows one tenant above the disclosure threshold, Pertamina Hulu Energi at 19.5% of revenue, down from a slightly higher share the year before [S19 p.79]. The LK states plainly that there was no related-party revenue in FY2025 or FY2024, which removes the channel that destroys value in most Indonesian family-controlled property names [S19 p.79, F31]. The workforce is small — about 190 people — because the buildings are managed through contractors and the landlord's own cost base is thin [S0].

Where RDTX sits in its market is the honest weak point. It is a sub-scale owner of four buildings in a city with hundreds, and it competes with listed landlords several times its size and with owner-occupier strata buildings that do not need to earn a yield [S15, S0]. Its advantage is location and vintage: Satrio and Simatupang are the corridors where multinational tenants cluster, and the buildings' original cost base means the group can cut rent further than a leveraged competitor before it loses money. Its disadvantage is the same vintage: the stock is not premium, and the market data show the premium tier filling while the rest competes on incentives [S15].

Strategy, as far as the filings show it, is to hold and let rather than to build. Capex in FY2025 was 3.1% of revenue, mostly fit-out and installations, and there is no announced development pipeline [S19 p.62, p.17]. Surplus cash has gone into a bond and time-deposit portfolio and into the dividend, not into new towers [S19 p.59]. For a shareholder that is a defensible choice — the return comes from the yield and the discount, not from growth — but it caps the upside: nothing in the current disclosure suggests the portfolio will grow other than through rent.

**The monetisation route we considered and did not use as the catalyst.** Four unencumbered, debt-free towers carried at IDR2,372.5bn of original cost against a capitalised value the RNAV puts well above that is the textbook setup for a sale-and-leaseback, a disposal at appraisal, or a DIRE-style listed vehicle. We assessed it on three tests and it fails the timing test. First, there is no announced transaction, no adviser mandate and no asset held for sale in the FY2025 accounts or the 2026 announcement file we archived, so a sale would have to be invented rather than dated [S19 p.62, S13, S17]. Second, the economics leak: the final tax on rent is charged on gross income, a disposal takes the corporate gain and withholding tax on the difference between cost and price, and a REIT structure would have to distribute at least nine-tenths of profit to qualify, none of which the group has signalled [S19 p.47]. Third, control: the controller holds 42.5% and the family stake is well above half, so a value-realising disposal is a decision the family makes for its own reasons, not one a minority can force [S2]. We therefore treat a sale or REIT as an upside we would pay for only when it is announced — the bull case credits the cash at face value but does not capitalise a disposal premium — and we keep the split as the nearest dated catalyst because it is the only one in the announcement record [S2, S19].

Indonesian office landlords of this generation typically own their towers through a single purpose
subsidiary, lease to corporate tenants on multi-year terms with service charges passed through, and
carry the buildings at cost under the historical-cost model rather than revaluing them. That
accounting choice keeps reported book value well below replacement cost and makes price-to-book a
poor guide to asset value; it also means depreciation is a real economic charge that has to be
restored before any cash-based multiple is computed. The Jakarta office market is cyclical with
long leads, because supply is decided years before demand arrives.

The Jakarta office market is past the bottom but not yet in a clean recovery. Colliers put demand for the whole of 2026 at 198,555 square metres and reported CBD occupancy of 76.3% in the third quarter, with Grade A at 78.0% and the Premium tier at 84.0%; some premium buildings are above nine-tenths occupied [S15]. The same note is careful about the quality of that demand: most transactions are still tenants moving between buildings rather than companies adding space, so net absorption is thinner than gross take-up [S15]. Vacancy is forecast to fall from 25.7% at the end of 2026 to 21.1% by 2029, a slow grind that depends on real demand rather than on relocations [S15].

What is changing is what tenants buy. Colliers describes a shift from flight-to-quality to flight-to-value: tenants still want better buildings, but they want to see the productivity gain justify the rent, and they increasingly want space that is ready to use because fit-out costs are themselves a capital burden [S15]. Building management quality, ESG credentials and total occupancy cost now sit alongside location in the decision [S15]. For a landlord of RDTX's vintage this cuts both ways: the group can win tenants who will not pay premium rents, but it has to keep investing in the buildings to stay in that conversation, which is why we carry capex at the last actual's share of revenue rather than letting it fade [S19 p.62].

The rate backdrop is the second industry driver and it is unhelpful for the sector in our house view. Bank Indonesia held its policy rate at 5.75 in October 2026 and raised the deposit facility instead, explicitly to defend the rupiah against external pressure, with inflation targeted at a narrow band around its medium-term goal [S20]. Our macro deck has real GDP growth at 5.3% and the rupiah path pressured at 18,350 to the dollar, and it classifies the regime as balance-of-payments pressure [deck.macro.bi_rate.spot]. Property is the most rate-sensitive sector on the exchange, and our firm-level tilt on Indonesian rate-sensitive property is to avoid it. We are not fighting that view: our rating on RDTX is HOLD with a 2.3% total return, a full step below the deck's AVOID only because the stock is not a geared developer. The tilt is about earnings and balance sheets that a funding squeeze can break; RDTX has no debt, no presales to fund and no construction commitment, so a higher discount rate hits the mark on its assets rather than its solvency, and the cash pile earns the higher rate instead of paying it. That is an exemption of transmission, not of direction: the same rate path is why we apply a wide cap rate, why the bear case widens it further, and why the target is a HOLD rather than the ADD a static-NAV model would have produced before this revision. To rate the shares above HOLD against the deck we would need evidence that the cap-rate cycle has turned in transactions, not just that the shares are cheap on our own mark.

Competitive structure is unfavourable on rivalry and favourable on new supply. Rivalry is high: with a quarter of the market empty, a landlord's pricing power depends on being in the right submarket, and tenants can and do move [S15]. Buyer power is high for the same reason, though it falls sharply for tenants who need a specific address or a particular floor plate [S15]. New supply in the prime corridors is constrained by land, which protects the long-run position of an owner with four standing assets [S19 p.62]. Supplier power is low — construction and services are competitive — and the threat of substitutes has shifted from home-working alone to a genuine preference for smaller, better, ready-to-use space, which reduces the total square metres a given headcount occupies [S15].

Regulation shapes the P&L more than it shapes the product. Income from leasing office space is subject to final income tax, applied to the gross value of the transaction and charged whether or not the landlord makes a profit; the LK records it as a separate line and trues it up against tax paid [S19 p.47, p.14]. For RDTX the charge was IDR57.0bn in FY2025 and it sits above the financing lines, so it behaves like a revenue levy: it grows with the top line even in a year when costs rise faster [S19 p.14]. There is no loss offset and no timing game available, which is one reason we do not model a low-tax bull case.

Market share is not disclosed and we will not invent it. What we can say is that RDTX is a price-taker in a market where the premium tier is rationed and the rest is oversupplied [S15]. Its moat is the land under the buildings and the cost basis of the structures; it is a real but narrow moat, worth the replacement cost of four Satrio-corridor towers and not a franchise multiple [S19 p.62, S7]. That is precisely the situation in which an asset-based valuation is the right primary method and an earnings multiple is a cross-check.

Jakarta's office market has historically moved in long cycles because supply is commissioned years
ahead of demand and because landlords rarely demolish. Service charges are typically passed through
to tenants at cost, so headline rent and net effective rent can diverge widely once incentives and
fit-out contributions are counted. Foreign tenants usually sign in United States dollars or with
dollar-linked escalation, which makes the sector sensitive to the rupiah even when the landlord
reports in local currency. ESG certification has become a leasing requirement for multinational
occupiers in the prime corridors.

The revenue base is stable and slowly growing. FY2025 revenue was IDR570.2bn, 7.5% higher year on year, with rent of IDR293.7bn and maintenance and power of IDR242.8bn carrying almost all of it [S19 p.79]. The first quarter of 2026 booked IDR142.1bn of revenue, about a point on the prior year, on flat operating costs [S10]. We model 2.0% for FY2026 and 3.0% thereafter, which is the last actual's run-rate plus the occupancy path Colliers describes rather than a rent spike [S15, S10].

The most important restatement in this report is depreciation. The data pack shows a depreciation charge of well under a billion rupiah, which is only the administrative piece; the audited LK charges IDR85.5bn of depreciation inside operational costs in FY2025 and IDR91.4bn in FY2024 [S19 p.79, S0]. We restate both years, which is why EBITDA is IDR433.1bn at a 76.0% margin rather than the figure the pack implies, and why EBIT stays at IDR347.6bn [S19]. Calibrating a cash cost off the pack's number would have overstated the operating margin by about a fifth of revenue; we have not done that.

Gross margin was 65.5% in FY2025 against 62.1% the year before, and we hold it at 65.5% rather than expanding it: the improvement came from lower building costs, not from pricing, and there is no reason to extrapolate it [S19 p.14]. Operating expenses were IDR25.7bn, 4.6% of revenue, and we hold them there; FY2024's higher ratio reflected a marketing charge that has not recurred [S19 p.80].

Below the operating line the structure is unusual and worth spelling out. The final tax of IDR57.0bn is deducted above pre-tax profit; finance income was IDR38.8bn on the cash and bond portfolio; and the remaining items netted to IDR-34.0bn [S19 p.14]. That reported line contains a IDR13.9bn one-off gain on the sale of other investments, which we strip out: the normalised line is the reported figure less that gain, and it is the normalised level we forecast. Its components — the final tax, tenants'-deposit discount amortisation, net rental income, the foreign exchange result, the loss on fixed-asset sales and dividend income — are held at their FY2025 amounts except the final tax, which moves with the statutory levy on forecast gross rent, giving IDR-49.2bn in FY2026. Holding the reported line flat instead, as a mechanical roll-forward would, carries the one-off gain into every year of the forecast and overstates earnings by roughly the size of that gain [S19 p.14]. The corporate tax charge left over is trivial and we keep the effective rate at 0.2% [S19 p.14, p.47]. That gives net profit of IDR355.0bn and earnings per share of Rp1,321, rising to Rp1,653 by FY2030. One mechanical note for anyone rebuilding the model: the template's development line is additive to the recurring base, so our forecast revenue carries the residual bucket twice — an overlap of under a billion rupiah a year, disclosed rather than netted out inside the engine [S19 p.79].

Cash generation is the strongest part of the story and the part that needs a caveat. Capex was IDR13.0bn of investment-property additions — land, buildings, installations and the project under construction in the note — plus IDR4.5bn of fixed-asset acquisitions [S19 p.62, p.17], 3.1% of revenue in total. The data pack's figure captures only the fixed-asset line and none of the investment-property spend, which is why we restate it rather than model around it [S0, F11]. Line convention, stated so the history can be read against this paragraph: the model's history capex line carries the investment-property additions only; the fixed-asset acquisitions are the separate investing line in the cash-flow statement and have to be added to it to reach the year's total cash capex [S19 p.62, p.17]. Their sum is the figure to compare with the forecast years, which are a single 3.1%-of-revenue line covering both. With the restated depreciation back in, free cash flow to the firm was IDR343.9bn against net profit of IDR351.1bn, so earnings are cash-backed [S19]. Working capital is structurally negative — unearned rent and tenant deposits exceed receivables — and we hold it at -30.0% of revenue, which releases cash as revenue grows rather than absorbing it [S19 p.13]. The caveat is that the model's cash balance compounds: it reaches IDR2,675.3bn by FY2030 on a 45.0% payout, against a market capitalisation of IDR3,319.7bn today. That is a real capability, not an error, but it means the valuation has to decide what the cash is worth — we credit it at face value in the RNAV and let the reader see that management will eventually have to raise the payout or buy something.

The balance sheet is the least risky in the sector. Cash and equivalents were IDR531.0bn and the current other-investments portfolio IDR611.1bn at the end of FY2025, with debt of IDR0.0bn: a net cash position, and the LK states that the group had no borrowings in either FY2025 or FY2024 [S19 p.12, p.89]. Equity is IDR3,299.1bn, investment properties are carried at IDR2,372.5bn on the cost model with no revaluation surplus, and there is no minority interest or lease liability worth modelling [S19 p.13, p.62]. Return on equity was 11.1%, low precisely because the asset base is carried at cost; on a marked-to-market asset base it would be lower still, which is the point of owning it at a discount rather than for the accounting return.

Capital allocation is a dividend plus a bond portfolio. The FY2025 dividend was Rp588 a share in total — a December interim and a final — a payout of 45.0% of earnings, and the final tranche of IDR104.3bn went ex in July 2026 out of the IDR158.1bn total [S9, S11, F37]. We hold the payout at 45.0%, in line with the record, and let cash accumulate rather than assume a special dividend we cannot date [S19 p.13].

Under the historical-cost model, depreciation of an investment property is charged on the structure
over its useful life and is a genuine economic cost in the sense that the building will eventually
need replacing, but it is not a cash cost in the year it is booked. That is why cash-based multiples
on a landlord have to add depreciation back and then subtract the capex needed to keep the building
lettable — the maintenance capex figure, not the accounting charge, is the real economic rent of the
asset. Indonesian filings print nil balances as a dash, which is why restating a zero balance
requires reading the absence of a line rather than a printed figure.

We value RDTX on net asset value, weighted 60.0% of the blend, with price-to-earnings and price-to-book as cross-checks at 20.0% each — the house method set for Indonesian property, and the right one here because the earnings are an annuity off a fixed asset base rather than a growth stream [S19, S15]. The group has no debt, so the WACC is the cost of equity, and the build is the engine's, in full: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4% less the 1.6% Indonesia sovereign default spread the house macro deck carries (the Damodaran series), plus a beta of 0.90 multiplied by the sum of a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5% — 11.9% in total [deck.macro.rf_idr, deck.macro.default_spread_id, deck.macro.erp_mature, deck.macro.crp_id]. The default-spread deduction is not a cosmetic adjustment: the risk-free rate here is a domestic government yield in a market that has defaulted within living memory, so the engine removes the sovereign credit component before adding an equity premium and the country risk premium, which is where the sovereign risk is charged. The beta of 0.90 is the property-developer default the config carries, not a fitted coefficient: at IDR47.0m of daily turnover any regression beta on this stock would be noise, and we prefer a stated industry default to a spurious number [S0].

The RNAV build starts from recurring gross profit and capitalises it at 8.5%. Because this LK deducts IDR85.5bn of building depreciation inside operational costs, the gross profit we capitalise is already net of depreciation, so 8.5% on gross profit is equivalent to a cash cap rate about a percentage point higher — the comparison a valuer would actually make [S19 p.79]. The cap rate is the largest judgement in this report and it is ours, not a sourced transaction: the Colliers note behind [S15], our industry source, gives occupancy, demand and rent negotiation but carries no cap rate, yield or transaction benchmark, and the peer set's median sits about a point above where we previously marked this name [S15]. We mark it at 8.5% on gross profit — the upper half of the cash-yield range the house property coverage set implies for a 76.3%-occupied, sub-scale, non-premium office landlord — rather than at the lower rate an appraisal of the premium tier would support. We add the cash and liquid portfolio at face value and deduct no debt. We also make the deduction the earlier draft missed: the tenant cash that is not ours. Current and non-current unearned rent of IDR180.6bn and IDR15.3bn, and current and non-current tenant deposits of IDR33.5bn and IDR94.5bn, are cash already sitting in the balance-sheet cash line, so a net asset value that adds the cash and ignores the obligation behind it double counts [S19 p.13]. The house property card requires advances to be deducted and we deduct them in full, through the negative land-value line of the engine bridge; the non-core legacy parcels in Bali and West Java sit in investment properties at a few billion rupiah of carrying value and are not worth an invented appraisal [S19 p.62]. That produces an RNAV method value of Rp16,249 a share after the 15.0% discount we apply to the asset value [S0, S2].

The discount is where judgement lives, and there are two layers, not one. The engine applies its 30.0% illiquidity haircut to the whole target, and we set 15.0% on the RNAV before that; the two compound, so the effective discount to the undiscounted assets is roughly two-fifths rather than the 15.0% headline. That is deliberate and it is the method, not a reverse-engineered number: the haircut is a constitutional deduction applied to any name whose three-month average daily turnover is below the lowest tier, and at IDR47.0m a day RDTX is far below it [S0]. The haircut falls on the market-derived legs as well as the asset leg, which we accept with a caveat: the P/E and P/BV values come from the same short own-history sample of this stock's traded record, so they already embed part of its illiquidity, and applying the haircut again is a second charge. We keep it because dropping it would mix a per-name liquidity premium into a house rule applied across the book, and because a target that leans on a thin sample of own-history multiples is the one that should least be grossed up. What we can measure of RDTX's own history is the multiple record, not a discount to appraised value — the company has never published an appraisal — and on that record the stock has traded near 1.1x book against 1.0x today [S0]. A five-year discount-to-RNAV band cannot be shown for this name because no NAV series exists; we say so rather than invent one, and anchor the discount on the peer band the house card sets for Indonesian developers.

The engine then rolls the blend forward one year at the cost of equity and deducts the expected dividend. That roll is worth about a tenth of the target and we show it rather than hide it: without it, the fundamental blend of Rp15,572 less the engine's 30.0% haircut is a value below today's Rp12,350 even before the Rp594 dividend, so the rating would still be HOLD at the bottom of the band. A property NAV does not compound at the cost of equity in reality — revenue grows at 3.0% in our forecast and the surplus cash accrues at a deposit rate — which is why we do not present the roll as fundamental appreciation: it is a twelve-month convention the engine applies to every name, and the rating does not depend on it. The value that does depend on our judgement is the cap rate, and we have marked it at a level the current price does not require us to defend.

The cross-checks sit below the asset value, and that is the interesting part of the table. Price-to-earnings gives Rp14,773 on a 11.3x forward multiple, and price-to-book gives Rp14,342 on 1.1x — both -9.1% and -11.7% respectively against the RNAV leg [S0]. We do not treat that as a contradiction. Book value is original cost from an era when these towers were new, so a multiple of book tells you almost nothing about asset value; and earnings multiples on a landlord ignore the depreciation that the cash flow adds back. The cross-checks are there to stop us overpaying for the asset story, and they do their job by pulling the blend down from Rp16,249 to Rp15,572.

The sensitivity grid in the industry template varies presales growth against the RNAV discount. For a pure landlord the presales axis is inert — there are no units to sell, and the residual bucket our template calls development revenue is a rounding item — so the live axis is the discount, and the second live driver is the cap rate, which the grid does not carry [S19 p.79]. We therefore read the table for the discount sensitivity only, and describe the cap-rate sensitivity in words: a cap rate a hundred basis points higher would take the RNAV leg down by about a tenth, which is the single largest swing in our target [S15].

What the price implies is a market that wants a yield and does not believe in the assets. At Rp12,350 the shares yield 4.8% forward and trade at 9.4x earnings and 5.0x EBITDA on the last actual balance sheet, for a debt-free portfolio with IDR531.0bn of cash plus IDR611.1bn of current investments [S0, S19]. The price appreciation we forecast is -2.5%; the rest of the total return is the dividend. In effect the market is demanding a high-teens cash yield on the buildings to own them in a stock it cannot trade in size, and we think that is too high a hurdle for assets with no refinancing risk — but not so obviously too high that we would pay up for the shares before the split has proven it can change the liquidity.

A note on the split for anyone using these numbers. Our target of Rp12,039 and every per-share figure here are on the old 268.8m share count, because the market price of Rp12,350 is dated 12 November 2026 and the data vendor was still quoting the pre-split level the next day: Rp12,775 on 13 November 2026 [S18, F44]. The exchange announcement of the new shares' trading start is not in the announcement file we archived, so we state the basis rather than assert a listing date [S13, S17]. Once the 5,380m post-split shares list, the equivalent target is a twentieth of that, and comparisons to the traded price should be made after adjusting one side or the other. If the new shares had listed before our price date, every per-share figure in this report would be out by the split factor, which is why the price is dated here and in the valuation tables.

The scenario set is deliberately symmetrical: the bear and the bull shock the same four drivers by mirrored amounts, so the range reflects the evidence rather than our mood [S15, S19]. The bear case takes forecast rent growth down five percentage points a year — a permanent loss of pricing power equivalent to the anchor tenant not renewing in a market that is 25.7% vacant, held through the forecast rather than recovered in year one — adds two hundred and twenty basis points to the cap rate toward the 2013 analogue, widens the discount by twelve points on a split that fails to deepen liquidity, and cuts the payout by fifteen points as cash flow is defended [S15, S2]. The bull case mirrors each of the four: growth five points higher as the recovery broadens into real absorption, the same cap-rate compression, the same discount narrowing, and a payout raised by the same fifteen points to a payout of 45.0% plus that amount, which is where the cash build described above starts being distributed rather than accumulated [S19 p.13]. The result is a bear value of Rp13,183, a base of Rp16,824 and a bull of Rp23,421 before the illiquidity haircut, weighted 40.0% to the base, 35.0% to the bear and 25.0% to the bull [S15, S19]. The base carries the largest weight but not a majority, and after the engine's 30.0% haircut the bear value sits below today's price while the bull carries the upside: the asymmetry in the outcomes comes from the discount interacting with the cap rate, not from asymmetric assumptions.

**Tenant concentration is the risk we can measure.** Pertamina Hulu Energi is 19.5% of revenue [S19 p.79]. A non-renewal at market rent is a first-year revenue hit of roughly a tenth to a fifth — the tenant is a fifth of revenue and the market is 25.7% vacant, so the space does not re-let at the same rent quickly — and the bear case models it as a permanent growth shock rather than a one-year dip, which is the harsher reading of the same evidence [S19 p.79, S15]. Likelihood is material over a twelve-month horizon and the impact is the largest single driver of the bear. The mitigation is that the group's cost base is low enough to re-let aggressively, and that the final tax falls with rent rather than against it.

**The buildings' competitiveness is the risk we cannot measure.** RDTX does not disclose portfolio occupancy, rent rolls or lease expiries, so we cannot verify whether its towers are tracking the 76.3% CBD average or lagging it [S19, S15]. We treat this as an evidence gap, not a neutral: the absence of disclosure in a market where the premium tier is visibly outperforming is itself a mild negative, and it is why we do not assume occupancy-led upside in the base case.

**Rates and the rupiah.** Property is the most rate-sensitive sector we cover and the house macro regime is balance-of-payments pressure with the policy rate at 5.75 [S20, deck.macro.bi_rate.lt]. RDTX has no debt, so the transmission is through the cap rate the market applies and through tenants' occupancy decisions, not through interest cover: each hundred basis points on the cap rate takes about a tenth off the RNAV leg, and the bear applies more than twice that, which is why a rate shock alone is not a minor scenario for this name.

**Liquidity is a structural risk, not a tail risk.** Turnover is IDR47.0m a day and the float is 21.1% [S0, S2]. An institution cannot build or exit a position without moving the price, which is exactly why the engine applies its 30.0% haircut and why our target embeds it. The split is intended to address this; whether it does is a twelve-month empirical question, and a failed split would leave the discount where it is.

**Governance and control.** The controller holds 42.5% and a second family holder takes the family stake well above half [S2, F27]. There is no related-party revenue, no debt to related parties, and the investment properties are at cost rather than revalued [S19 p.79, p.62]. The risks that remain are the ordinary ones for a controlled Indonesian company: a dividend policy that can change, a strategy that can diversify into unrelated assets, and a market that will not pay for the assets while the float stays thin.

**Tax and earnings quality.** The final tax is levied on gross rent, so a rent cut reduces revenue and profit in almost the same proportion and there is no loss shield [S19 p.47]. Separately, the first-quarter headline growth was non-operational: net profit of IDR103.7bn included a IDR19.2bn gain on investment sales, and revenue grew about a point [S10]. We have excluded that class of gain from the base case, which means our FY2026 earnings are lower than a headline-extrapolating model would show.

Signposts that would change the view: a portfolio occupancy or rent-roll disclosure that shows the buildings at or above the CBD average; evidence that the split has multiplied turnover and narrowed the bid-ask spread; a dividend increase or a special payout from the cash pile; a cap-rate compression visible in transactions; or, on the other side, a large tenant giving back space.

RDTX is a controlled company and the register is stable. Sutiadi Widjaja holds 42.5%, Turniady Widjaja holds a further stake just under a fifth, and the free float is 21.1% of the pre-split count [S2]. The insider share in the data pack is 78.8%, consistent with the registry breakdown, and there is no institutional holding of note [S0, S2]. The one-for-twenty split approved on 4 November 2026 was carried without a dissenting vote and takes the nominal value from five hundred rupiah to twenty-five, lifting the share count to 5,380m [S2]. That is a liquidity measure, not a change in control: the family's percentage stakes are unchanged.

Related-party flows, the channel that usually matters on this exchange, appear absent. The LK states that there was no revenue from related parties in FY2025 or FY2024, the group has no borrowings at all, and the only related-party balances are the ordinary intercompany ones that eliminate on consolidation [S19 p.79, p.89, F31]. We also found no pledge of the controlling stake in the disclosures we reviewed, and nothing in the announcement record points to a special notation or the monitoring board — a check we run before committing estimates, because a call-auction board would invalidate every entry and exit assumption [S0, S2, S17].

Two governance caveats. First, the audited FY2025 statements carry an independent auditor's report, but the opinion pages were not text-extractable in our archived copy, so we cannot quote the opinion or name the firm; the statements themselves are internally consistent, and we flag the gap rather than assert more than we can source [S19 p.1]. Second, the buildings are carried at cost with no revaluation, which is conservative and keeps price-to-book honest, but it also means shareholders have no independent appraisal of the portfolio to test our cap rate against [S19 p.62].

The dividend record is the governance feature shareholders actually experience, and it needs one timing point. Cash paid out during FY2025 was IDR115.2bn, which was the FY2024 distribution; the FY2025 dividend of Rp588 a share, a payout of 45.0% of earnings, was declared on FY2025 profit and paid after the year end, with the final dividend of IDR104.3bn going ex in July 2026 and the IDR158.1bn total split between a December interim and that final [S19 p.17, S9, S11, F37]. The pattern is an interim each December and a final after the annual meeting, and the amounts have been stable rather than a promise [S17]. With the cash balance rising we see room for the distribution to grow without new debt [S19 p.13].

On ESG the exposure is buildings. Tenants increasingly weigh energy performance and certification in letting decisions, and Colliers explicitly lists ESG among the factors shaping demand in the prime corridors [S15]. Retrofitting older stock is a capital call the group can fund from cash but has not yet announced, and it is one of the reasons we hold capex at the last actual's share of revenue rather than letting it decline [S19 p.62]. Social and governance controversies are not visible in the sources reviewed; the concentration of ownership is the governance fact that matters, and it is priced.

Family-controlled Indonesian property companies are commonly used as vehicles for the controlling
family's other interests, which is why related-party land purchases and construction contracts are
the standard thing to check. Roda Vivatex is unusual in having no related-party revenue and no
borrowings, which removes the two most common leakages. The exchange's special monitoring board and
its notation letters are the first thing to check on any small cap, because a name on that board
trades in call auctions and cannot be entered or exited in size at the screen price.

The nearest catalyst is the split. The EGM approved it on 4 November 2026 and the shares were changed from a par value of five hundred rupiah to twenty-five, with the issued count rising to 5,380m [S2]. The trading start of the new shares is not in the announcement file we archived, and our price is dated before any listing that we can source, so the first thing to watch is the exchange's listing announcement and then whether daily value traded rises in the weeks after it [S13, S17, S0]. An asset sale, sale-and-leaseback or DIRE structure would be the value-realising catalyst we actually want, but nothing in the record points to one being prepared, so we list it as a signpost rather than a dated event [S19 p.62].

The second dated event is the FY2026 audited accounts and the dividend resolution that follows them, in the statutory window after the year end. That report is where the office cycle shows up in RDTX's own numbers rather than in Colliers' market data: rent per square metre, the maintenance and power line, and whether the group discloses occupancy [S19, S15]. We will compare FY2026 revenue against our IDR582.5bn and net profit against IDR355.0bn, and we will hold management to the cash build we forecast.

The third is the market data itself. Colliers' quarterly occupancy and vacancy readings, and any evidence of prime-corridor rent reversions, are the best available proxy for a portfolio we cannot see [S15]. We monitor the KPI set below, and we will treat a move of more than a tenth in the target as a reason to re-underwrite rather than to tweak.

Between updates we watch five things: portfolio occupancy or rent-roll disclosure when it comes; the maintenance and power revenue line as a proxy for occupied space; the investment-property additions line as a proxy for whether management is defending the buildings' competitiveness; the cash balance and the payout ratio, since the two together decide whether the discount has a reason to narrow; and turnover and free float after the split [S19, S2, S0].

bear.narrative: Jakarta office demand stalls as tenants keep consolidating. The Pertamina-anchored lease at Menara PHE is not renewed on the same terms - the largest tenant is 19.5% of revenue and the market vacancy is 25.7% - so revenue falls in the first year and the portfolio is re-let only at lower rent, permanently. At the same time the BI tightening regime lifts the cap rate by 220bp toward the 2013 analogue and the 1:20 split fails to deepen liquidity, leaving the market's discount at the wide end. Management defends cash flow by cutting the payout by fifteen points. The four shocks compound rather than offset.

bull.narrative: The 2026 office recovery broadens into real absorption, so rent reversions turn positive on the Satrio corridor and RDTX Place re-lets at higher rates; the 1:20 split brings retail liquidity and a re-rating; and with the cash pile compounding management lifts the payout from 45% by the mirrored fifteen points rather than sitting on it, so the dividend stream the market actually prices is materially higher.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs presales growth and RNAV discount

assumptions.label: Presales growth
assumptions.basis: Not applicable: RDTX sells no property units, it is a pure office landlord [S19 p.19]. The template's presales line carries only the LK's residual "others" revenue bucket (under Rp1bn of parking/overtime-type income), held flat, so no marketing-sales cycle exists to grow.

assumptions.label: Share of presales recognised in the same year
assumptions.basis: No handover lag exists for a landlord: rent and service charges are recognised over the lease term [S19 p.45], so the residual bucket is recognised as billed and the split convention is immaterial.

assumptions.label: Recurring revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the last actual and the market: Q1-2026 revenue grew 1.2% yoy [S10], Jakarta CBD office occupancy reached 76.3% in Q3-2026 with Grade A near 78% and Premium near 84% [S15], and FY2022-FY2025 revenue compounded at about 3.8% [S19]. FY2026 takes the Q1 run-rate, then about 3% nominal as occupancy firms and premium-grade landlords regain pricing power [S15].

assumptions.label: Development gross margin
assumptions.basis: Not applicable (no development revenue); set equal to the recurring margin so the residual bucket carries the group's building-level margin rather than an invented spread [S19 p.79].

assumptions.label: Recurring gross margin
assumptions.basis: Held at the last actual: the LK shows gross margin of 65.5% in FY2025 against 62.1% in FY2024, after building operating costs that include Rp85.5bn of investment-property depreciation [S19 p.14, p.79]. No margin expansion is assumed; revenue and property costs grow together.

assumptions.label: Cap rate for investment property (RNAV)
assumptions.basis: Applied to gross profit, which in this LK is already net of Rp85.5bn of building depreciation [S19 p.79], so 8.5% here equals about a 9.9% cap rate on cash net operating income after the model's maintenance capex - the upper half of the cash-yield range the house property coverage set implies for income assets, whose median is 9.3% on gross profit. The earlier 7.3% was the lowest in that 17-name set and could not be sourced: S15 gives occupancy and demand but no cap rate or transaction yield [S15]. 8.5% is a house judgement, labelled as one, and sits at the midpoint of the 8.0-8.7% range consistent with a 9.3-10% cash yield for a 76%-occupied, sub-scale office landlord whose stock is not premium grade [S15, S19].

assumptions.label: Target discount to RNAV
assumptions.basis: This is not a 15% target discount to appraised value: the engine then applies its own 30% illiquidity haircut to the whole target (ADTV of Rp47m is below its lowest tier), so the two layers compound to an effective discount of roughly two-fifths to RNAV - close to the 40-70% band in which IDX developers trade [S0]. We set the first layer at 15% so the post-haircut target does not double-count the illiquidity the market already prices; a further widening to the peer-median 40% RNAV discount on top of the 30% haircut would imply a discount the stock has never traded at. The discount is expected to narrow only modestly on the office cycle turning (CBD occupancy 76.3%, Premium 84%) [S15], the 1:20 split approved 4 November 2026 [S2] and a covered yield [S0]; with the 42.51% controlling stake and 21.14% float there is no force that closes the gap inside twelve months [S2]. Section 4 states the effective discount and the no-roll value explicitly.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating expenses were 4.5% of revenue (Rp25.7bn, of which Rp2.1bn selling) [S19 p.80]; FY2024's 6.7% was inflated by Rp10.3bn of marketing fees. Held at the last actual.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: depreciation charged in operational costs was Rp85.5bn (15.0% of revenue) in FY2025 and Rp91.4bn in FY2024 [S19 p.79]. The pack's Rp0.6bn is only the admin charge and would overstate EBITDA by about a quarter.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total FY2025 cash capex was Rp17.568bn: Rp13.024bn of investment-property additions - land, buildings, installations and Rp4.292bn of project under construction [S19 p.62, F11] - plus Rp4.544bn of fixed-asset acquisitions [S19 p.17, F36], or 3.1% of revenue. The pack's Rp4.5bn captures only the fixed-asset line. Held at 3.1% with no new-build pipeline: the spend is fit-out and building upkeep, not expansion.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital is structural for a landlord: unearned rent and tenant deposits of Rp210bn against small receivables [S19 p.13]. FY2025 net working capital was -30% of revenue.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Residual only. Office rental income is taxed finally at 10% of gross revenue, shown in the LK as a separate Rp57.0bn line above pre-tax profit [S19 p.14, p.47]; that charge sits in other non-operating below. The remaining corporate charge was Rp0.24bn, 0.07% of pre-tax profit.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The group is debt-free: no bank borrowings at 31 December 2025 and finance costs nil [S19 p.14], so the input only covers the legacy finance-lease tail.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of Rp38.8bn on opening cash of Rp887bn in FY2025 implies 4.4% [S19 p.14], consistent with time-deposit rates; held flat as the house rate path peaks.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No borrowing assumed: the group has been net cash since FY2024 and funds capex and dividends from operating cash flow [S19 p.13].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt line by line from the FY2025 P&L [S19 p.14]. The actual line is -Rp34.033bn, but it contains a Rp13.898bn one-off gain on the sale of other investments [S19 p.14]; excluding that gain, the normalised FY2025 level is -Rp47.930bn: final rental tax -Rp57.019bn plus tenants'-deposit discount amortisation -Rp2.486bn, net rental income +Rp8.338bn, FX gain +Rp0.642bn, loss on fixed-asset sales -Rp0.506bn, dividend income +Rp2.977bn and other net +Rp0.123bn. FY2026 keeps every component at its FY2025 level except the final tax, which moves with the 10% gross-revenue levy to -Rp58.254bn, giving -Rp49.165bn; the later years follow the same arithmetic. Holding the line at the reported -Rp34.033bn, as the red team alternatively suggests, would keep a one-off investment gain in the base case and overstate earnings by about Rp14bn; we rebuild rather than hold.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The two operating subsidiaries are 99.99% owned and minority interest on the balance sheet is nil [S19 p.20, p.13], so essentially all profit accrues to parent shareholders.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The June 2026 AGMS paid out Rp158.05bn on FY2025 profit of Rp351.06bn, a 45% payout split between a Rp200 interim and a Rp388 final [S11]; held at 45%, in line with the FY2024 record.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No new shares: the 1:20 split approved on 4 November 2026 takes 268.8m shares to 5.38bn with no change in capital raised [S2], so it is a per-share presentation change, not dilution.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Office rents are an inflation-linked stream; 3% sits just below the house long-run Indonesian CPI deck and matches the recurring growth path used in the forecast years.

challenges.challenge: Fact F11, capex FY2025A of Rp25.267bn, quotes a line from the investment-property accumulated-depreciation schedule: Installations 230,090,375,924 + 25,267,672,910 = 255,358,048,834 is a depreciation charge, not capex. The LK cash flow shows FY2025 acquisition of fixed assets of Rp4.544bn plus investment properties of Rp10.249bn, or Rp14.79bn (S19 p.17), and the cost movement adds Rp4.29bn of project under construction (p.62). The 4.4% capex_pct and the justification that clears the restatement.capex BLOCK therefore rest on a misread.
challenges.answer: F11 replaced: 13.024bn is the note 9 investment-property additions, not the accumulated-depreciation movement; F36 adds 4.544bn of fixed assets, so total FY2025 cash capex is 17.568bn [S19]. capex_pct is 3.1% and the five-times claim is withdrawn.

challenges.challenge: The 7.3% cap rate is the valuation's largest input and its stated basis is not in the source. S15, the 6,686-character Colliers note, covers occupancy, demand and rent negotiation only; it carries no cap rate, yield or Jakarta CBD Grade A band for 2002-2012 stock. The 7.3% on gross profit is 8.44% on cash NOI before the model's own Rp26.4bn maintenance capex and 7.95% after it - about 50bp over the 7.45% 10Y SUN - for a 76%-occupied, sub-scale office landlord in a sector the house deck marks AVOID. It is also the lowest cap rate in the 17-name PROPERTY_DEVELOPERS peer set, whose median is 9.3%.
challenges.answer: Cap rate raised from 7.3% to 8.5% on gross profit as a labelled house judgement, because S15 carries occupancy and demand but no cap rate or transaction yield [S15]. It equals about a 9.9% cash yield after maintenance capex, the upper half of the 9.3-10% peer range; the model and target are re-run at it.

challenges.challenge: The target rolls the fundamental blend forward at COE: 17,621 x 1.1185 - 594 = 19,116 before the 30% haircut. That assumes a static four-tower portfolio plus cash compounds at 11.85% a year, while the model itself grows revenue at 3% and NAV at roughly 4-5%. The roll contributes about Rp2,088/share gross and Rp1,494/share after the DPS deduction, or 8.5pp of the 15.1% total return. Without it the probability-weighted blend is 17,922, the target 12,545 and the total return 6.4%, a HOLD.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now shows the no-roll value: the blend less the engine's 30% haircut is below today's price even before the dividend, so the rating is HOLD with or without the cost-of-equity roll, which is labelled a twelve-month engine convention rather than NAV appreciation [S0].

challenges.challenge: The house property card defines RNAV as assets less net debt less advances, but the engine adds cash of Rp863.5bn and deducts nothing for the Rp210bn of unearned rent and tenant deposits the report itself cites in section 3. The deposit cash is inside the cash balance, so RNAV double counts it. Deducting the Rp210bn removes about Rp660/share from RNAV and Rp300-350/share from the target.
challenges.answer: All tenant advances are deducted in the RNAV bridge: current and non-current unearned rent F40/F41 and tenant deposits F42/F43, 323.9bn at 31 December 2025, because that cash is already in the cash line [S19 p.13]. The 30% haircut then falls on the lower RNAV.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative names a Pertamina Hulu Energi non-renewal at Menara PHE, but the shock set only cuts growth to -1%/0%. Pertamina is 19.5% of revenue, Rp111bn; at the 25.7% market vacancy in S15 a first-year revenue hit of 10-19% is the realistic range, not the mid-single-digit the risk section asserts. The bear value of 15,959, down 16% from base, is therefore milder than the risk the report itself describes.
challenges.answer: The bear now takes forecast growth down five points a year, a permanent pricing-power loss harsher than a one-year hit, grounded in Pertamina at 19.5% of revenue and market vacancy of 25.7% [S19, S15]. The bull mirrors it at plus five points.

challenges.challenge: The only rate shock is +120bp on a 7.3% cap rate in a balance-of-payments-pressure regime (BI 5.75, rupiah 18,350, 10Y SUN 7.45%). data/base_rates.yaml property_nav_discount_narrowing records base_down_pct of -25% over 2.5 years and warns the current BI tightening is a live headwind. A 200-300bp cap widening, the 2013 analogue, and a failed split that leaves the discount at 47% are both absent.
challenges.answer: The bear now adds 220bp to the cap rate toward the 2013 analogue and widens the RNAV discount by twelve points on a split that fails to deepen liquidity, with the payout cut fifteen points [S15, S2]. Base probability is 40%.

challenges.challenge: The model accumulates Rp2,631bn of cash by FY2030 on a 45% payout, about 79% of today's market capitalisation, yet no scenario values a higher payout or a special dividend. The bull narrative mentions a special dividend or a new acquisition, but its three shocks contain no payout or bridge item. The most concrete upside in the model is neither capitalised nor bridged.
challenges.answer: The bull lifts the payout by the mirrored fifteen points to 60% and the report now states that the cash build is distributed rather than accumulated; the bull value of 23,421 pre-haircut against a base of 16,824 captures it [S19 p.13].

challenges.challenge: Four unencumbered, debt-free towers carried at cost of Rp2.5trn against a capitalised value of Rp5.4trn is the textbook setup for monetisation - a sale-and-leaseback, a DIRE/REIT or an asset sale at appraisal - which the house property card names as a standard discount catalyst. The report does not discuss it, and its chosen catalyst, the 1:20 split, is a share-count change that upstreams no value; data/base_rates.yaml holdco_discount_narrowing explicitly says such a discount plus a non-value catalyst is not a thesis.
challenges.answer: Section 1 now assesses sale-and-leaseback, disposal at appraisal and a DIRE vehicle, sets out the tax leakage and family-control constraints, and records that no transaction is announced in the accounts or announcement file [S19 p.62, S13, S17]. The split stays the nearest dated catalyst.

challenges.challenge: The 30% illiquidity haircut is applied to the whole target, but 40% of the blend is own-history PE and PBV values (11.3x, 1.12x) derived from the same stock's traded prices, which already embed its illiquidity; haircutting them again understates the target by roughly Rp2.0-2.3k/share, about 15%. Separately, the 15% RNAV discount is set so the total lands near 40%, reverse-engineered to the market's existing 47%, and is the second-lowest of 17 property peers against a median of 40%, with no own five-year discount band shown as the method card requires.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now shows the two layers compounding to roughly two-fifths, justifies the constitutional haircut on market-derived legs rather than removing it, and gives the own-history multiple record of 1.1x book versus 1.0x today because no appraisal series exists for a five-year NAV band [S0].

challenges.challenge: Several typed figures in the prose do not survive checking: real GDP growth at 529.0%, where deck.macro.gdp_real_id spot is 5.29%; market capitalisation of IDR3,319,680,000.00tn, which should be Rp3.32trn; 0.9x book, where 12,350/12,273 is 1.0x; 4.3x EBITDA, which uses FY2026E net cash of Rp1,404.9bn and is 5.6x on the spot balance sheet; the final tranche of IDR158.1bn, where S9 shows the final dividend as Rp104.29bn or Rp388 and Rp158.05bn is the FY2025 total; and cash of IDR1,142.1bn, where S19 p.12 shows cash and equivalents of Rp531.0bn plus other investments of Rp611.1bn.
challenges.answer: Every flagged figure is re-based: GDP now pctv at 5.3%, market cap idrb, book multiple on FY2025A, EV/EBITDA on the last actual balance sheet, final dividend F37 of 104.29bn, and cash split into F38 plus F39 [S18, S19]. Lint passes.

challenges.challenge: The cost-of-equity sentence does not reproduce its own 11.9%: 7.45% + 0.90 x 4.23% + 2.46% = 13.7%, not 11.85%. The engine actually uses rf 7.45% minus a 1.62% default spread plus 0.90 x (4.23% + 2.46%) = 11.85%, so the -1.62pp adjustment is undisclosed and the 0.90 beta is an industry default applied to a stock with Rp47m ADTV. Because the target is rolled at COE, the reader cannot reproduce the largest mechanical input.
challenges.answer: The cost-of-equity sentence now reproduces the engine exactly: rf 7.45% less a 1.62% Indonesia sovereign default spread from the Damodaran macro deck, plus 0.90 times (4.23% mature ERP plus 2.46% country premium), equals 11.85% [S0]. The 0.90 beta is the property default because 47m ADTV makes a regression beta noise.

challenges.challenge: Every per-share figure is on the pre-split 268.8m count, and the Rp12,350 price is dated 12 November 2026, seven days after the 1:20 split was approved on 4 November. The report asserts the traded price and data pack are pre-split without citing the exchange announcement of the listing or trading start, and section 7 admits the listing date is unknown. If the new shares list before the price date, the price, target and every ratio are 20x out.
challenges.answer: The price basis is proved by the data vendor's own quote: F44 shows 12,775 on 13 November 2026, still the pre-split level [S18]. The exchange announcement of the trading start is absent from S13 and S17, so the report states the basis and the risk rather than asserting a listing date.

challenges.challenge: The deck classifies the regime as balance-of-payments pressure, marks property AVOID and CAUTIOUS, and the base-rate notes warn that the current BI tightening is a live headwind. The report writes that it is not fighting that view and then rates ADD on a 6pp discount narrowing. It also misreads deck.macro.gdp_real_id as 529.0%. The section reads the deck's variables but does not reconcile a positive rating with its sector tilt.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now reconciles the rating with the deck: HOLD is a step below the deck's AVOID because the exemption is transmission, not direction - no debt, no presales, and cash that earns the higher rate; an above-HOLD rating needs transaction cap-rate evidence [S20].

challenges.challenge: Other non-operating items jump from -34.03 in FY2025A to -49.4 in FY2026E, a 45% step, and the stated build does not sum: -57.0 final tax + 2.49 deposit amortisation + 8.34 net rental + 2.98 dividend = -43.2, not -49.4. Holding the line at FY2025's -34.0 would add about Rp15bn to net profit, or Rp57 per share, 4% of the target.
challenges.answer: Other non-operating items are rebuilt line by line: the reported -34.03bn contains a 13.90bn one-off investment gain (new F45) [S19 p.14]; the normalised components sum to -47.93bn and FY2026E is -49.2bn with the final tax at 10% of forecast gross rent. Holding the reported line would keep the one-off gain.

challenges.challenge: FY2025A capex in the model is 13.02bn while the report s3 total and the capex_pct basis state 17.568bn (13.024bn investment-property additions plus 4.544bn fixed-asset acquisitions, F36); the history column understates FY2025A capex by 26% and FCFF by about 4.5bn, and QC finding Q1 (FIX) is still unanswered.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The history capex line is the note 9 investment-property addition (F11, 13.024bn) and the 4.544bn fixed-asset acquisition (F36) is a separate investing line; rather than force a summed number no single filing quote supports, s3 now annotates the line convention beside it and states the two are additive to total cash capex, with forecast years at 3.1% of revenue. Target unchanged at 12,039.

missing_bull_case.note: No value for the Rp2.6trn cash build by FY2030 or for a higher payout, and no REIT or asset-sale route for four unencumbered towers. The chosen catalyst, the 1:20 split, is a share-count change and data/base_rates.yaml says a cheap discount plus a non-value catalyst is not a thesis.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear names a Pertamina Hulu Energi non-renewal (19.5% of revenue) but does not model it; the rate shock is only +120bp against a house AVOID and a 38% base rate; and a failed split leaving the 47% discount in place is absent from the scenario set.

assumption_realism.note: Cap rate is the lowest of 17 property peers (7.3% on gross profit, 8.44% cash, 7.95% after maintenance capex); the 15% RNAV discount is the second-lowest in the peer set; base probability 50% exceeds the 38% house archetype; the capex basis rests on a misread line.

evidence_and_citations.note: F11 and F17 capex misread; typed prose numbers fail checking (529.0% GDP, 3,319,680,000.00tn market cap, 0.9x book, 4.3x EBITDA, 158.1bn final dividend, 1,142.1bn cash); F29's debt zero is cited to a receivables-aging quote.

valuation_method_fit.note: RNAV omits the Rp210bn tenant deposits and unearned rent the house card deducts as advances; the 12-month roll at COE assumes a static portfolio compounds at 11.85%; the COE sentence does not reproduce 11.9%; the split's trading date and price basis are unverified.

bias_and_tone.note: The ADD is driven by the mechanical COE roll: strip it and the probability-weighted target is 12,545, a 6.4% total return, i.e. HOLD. The bear is milder than the report's own risk narrative, so the prose claims more than the scenarios test.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The deck marks the regime balance-of-payments pressure, property AVOID and CAUTIOUS with no evidence to narrow, and the base-rate notes flag the BI tightening as a headwind. The report says it is not fighting that view, then rates ADD on a 6pp narrowing, and misreads deck GDP as 529.0%.

conservatism_audit.note: The 30% illiquidity haircut is applied to PE and PBV legs that are already market-derived, worth roughly Rp2.0-2.3k/share; the 15% RNAV discount is reverse-engineered to a 40% total with no own five-year band; FY2026 other non-operating items step up 45% with a build that does not sum.

flags.message: capex FY2025A restated at 2.87x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's FY2025 capex of Rp4.544bn is only the cash acquisition of fixed assets. The LK's investment-property cost movement shows a further Rp13.024bn of additions in FY2025 - land Rp1.948bn, buildings Rp2.854bn, installations Rp3.930bn and Rp4.292bn of project under construction [S19 p.62] - so total cash capex was Rp17.568bn, 3.1% of revenue, not 0.8%. The engine's FY2025A capex line carries the Rp13.024bn investment-property component (F11) and the Rp4.544bn fixed-asset component is disclosed as F36; the pack understates capex by a factor of about four, not the factor of five the earlier draft claimed. The restated D&A of Rp85.5bn and this capex still reproduce the LK's closing cash once the dividend is deducted [S19 p.17].
